# Publishing and Subscribing

Alice opens the lecture page while the lecturer is already speaking. Her browser connects to a relay, but the relay cannot yet know which lecture she wants. Even after it learns that, it still needs to know whether she wants audio, video, or both.

A subscription supplies that information. It asks another endpoint to deliver objects from a named track. In this chapter we will follow Alice's request from the first connection through playback, then see what changes when another viewer joins.

## Finding the lecture

The application must first turn Alice's choice into track names. The lecture page might already contain a publication name, or it might use namespace discovery to find available publishers. Discovery supplies information about what is available within the service; the application decides how to present that information as a room list, an invitation, or a public directory.

Once it finds the publication, the player reads its media description. This tells it which tracks contain audio and which contain video **renditions**: alternative encodings, such as low-resolution and high-resolution video. Alice's player can start by choosing audio and a low-resolution rendition. We will examine that media description in the browser chapter.

Discovery and delivery can have different access rules. A private lecture might be hidden from the room list as well as unavailable for playback. Knowing its name does not grant permission to receive it. MOQT provides [namespace discovery mechanisms](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-4); the service supplies the access policy.

## Establishing a session

Before Alice and the relay can exchange requests, they need a compatible MoQ session. A session is the protocol relationship in which the endpoints exchange requests and content. The transport carries that conversation, but it does not interpret its messages.

In MOQT draft-21, version selection happens during transport establishment. Native QUIC uses ALPN, a handshake field identifying the application protocol; WebTransport uses its protocol negotiation header. The identifier for this edition's draft is `moqt-21`. This is why a working network path is only part of establishing a connection: the endpoints must also agree on the protocol they will speak. See [§6.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-6.2).

Each endpoint opens a control stream and starts it with `SETUP`, exchanging session options and supported extensions. Each control stream is **unidirectional**: only the endpoint that opened it sends on it. A request such as `SUBSCRIBE` uses a separate **bidirectional** stream, so the other endpoint can answer on that same stream. Objects travel separately from these request messages.

The implementation can overlap some of this work. Requests and data may be sent while initialization is still underway, with early arrivals buffered until setup completes. The separate steps explain their responsibilities, rather than imposing a round trip for each one. See [§6.3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-6.3).

### From a connection to the first object

This sequence follows a direct-QUIC session after its transport handshake. The browser path first establishes a WebTransport session. Stream labels describe their jobs, not numeric QUIC stream IDs.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: MoQ session setup and first subscription delivery
    accDescr: After transport establishment, client and relay each send SETUP on their own control stream. The client opens a bidirectional request stream for SUBSCRIBE, the relay answers SUBSCRIBE_OK there, and sends objects on separate subgroup streams.
    participant C as Client
    participant R as Relay
    Note over C,R: Transport established with compatible MoQ version
    C->>R: Client control stream: SETUP
    R->>C: Relay control stream: SETUP
    C->>R: New request stream: SUBSCRIBE track
    R->>C: Same request stream: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    R->>C: Separate subgroup stream: objects
    R->>C: Another subgroup stream: more objects
```

The picture shows one successful ordering, not mandatory waits between every arrow. Setup, requests, and data can overlap under the draft's initialization rules. Discovery is omitted because this client already knows the track name. `SUBSCRIBE_OK` accepts a request; it does not mean the first picture has been decoded. The separate streams are specified in [draft-21 §6.4](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-6.4).

## Asking for audio

Alice's player sends `SUBSCRIBE`, naming the lecture's audio track and specifying its delivery choices. The relay answers with `SUBSCRIBE_OK` if it accepts, or `REQUEST_ERROR` if it rejects the request. Acceptance establishes the subscription; the audio itself arrives as objects on the data path.

Suppose the relay is not yet receiving this lecture. The service has associated the publication with an upstream publisher through registration, routing configuration, or implementation-specific discovery. The relay uses that information to make an upstream subscription of its own; a track name is not an Internet-wide lookup service. The following example begins after setup and shows one possible sequence. Both subscriptions request compatible delivery settings.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A viewer subscribes through a relay
    accDescr: Alice subscribes to audio at the relay. The relay obtains an upstream subscription from the publisher, accepts Alice's request, and forwards audio objects.
    participant A as Alice
    participant R as Relay
    participant P as Publisher
    A->>R: SUBSCRIBE audio
    R->>P: SUBSCRIBE audio
    P-->>R: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    R-->>A: SUBSCRIBE_OK
    P->>R: Audio objects
    R->>A: Audio objects
```

Alice's subscription and the relay's upstream subscription belong to different sessions. The relay receives objects as a subscriber, then supplies them to Alice as a publisher. It may already have an upstream subscription or cached content, so every new viewer need not cause this whole exchange.

Now Bob opens the same lecture and asks for the same audio. The relay can reuse its upstream content while maintaining a separate downstream subscription for Bob. If Alice leaves, Bob still needs that content. If both leave, and no recorder or other consumer remains, the relay can cancel its upstream request. This is how a relay combines demand without making every viewer share one connection. See [§7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-7).

The publisher can initiate a subscription too, by offering a track with `PUBLISH`. The receiver accepts with `REQUEST_OK`—called `PUBLISH_OK` when accepting a publication in this draft—or rejects with `REQUEST_ERROR`. A relay must already know the client is interested in and authorized for that content. Either direction of initiation establishes the same kind of subscription. See [§3.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-3.1).

## Joining video in the middle

Audio is arriving, and Alice's player also requests video. The publisher is halfway through group 42. In our example, the group's first object contains a keyframe and the later frames depend on earlier pictures. Receiving only the next new frame may therefore leave Alice with bytes she cannot decode.

The player can retrieve the beginning of group 42 while following new objects, or wait for the next independent group. The first choice can start playback sooner if the missing content is available and quick to deliver. The second avoids catching up through the current group, but waits for a new decoding starting point.

A **fetch** requests a bounded portion of a track. In draft-21, a standalone `FETCH` receives `FETCH_OK` or `REQUEST_ERROR`; fetched objects use a separate data stream. Successful delivery finishes when that data stream ends. Acceptance tells the requester that its request was accepted, rather than that every object has already arrived. See [§3.2.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-3.2.1).

For Alice's first choice, draft-21 also allows `FILL_PARAMETERS` on the subscription. These request a bounded fill range on a fetch stream alongside ongoing subscription delivery. The ranges can overlap, so the player must handle duplicate objects; pairing a fill through the largest known object with a subscription starting at the next object avoids that overlap. For the second choice, a location filter can start delivery at the next group. A **location** is a group ID and object ID: a position in the track, rather than a clock reading. See [fill ranges (§3.4)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-3.4) and [location filters (§3.3.1)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-3.3.1).

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Two ways to join a video track
    accDescr: Alice joins during group 42. She can retrieve its earlier objects and follow new ones, or wait for the independently decodable group 43. Either route needs codec configuration before decoding.
    J["Alice joins during group 42"] --> C["Retrieve earlier objects in group 42"]
    J --> W["Wait for group 43"]
    C --> F["Combine with ongoing delivery"]
    W --> K["Receive group 43 from its keyframe"]
    F --> D["Decode with the codec configuration"]
    K --> D
```

Filling the current group uses retained data; starting with the next group waits for new data. Neither route can promise an immediate picture. Retained objects take time to transfer, and the next keyframe may not have been produced yet.

Both choices depend on the media format identifying usable starting points. Switching from low-resolution to high-resolution video raises the same question: where can the decoder begin using the new rendition?

Fetching also depends on retention. The relay may have discarded the beginning of group 42, or never received it. To offer a “rewind 30 seconds” button, the service must retain enough content and map playback time to track locations. The fetch mechanism provides a way to request that content; storage and timing information make the feature possible.

## Ending a subscription

When Alice disables video, her player should cancel the video subscription while leaving audio active. Otherwise, the relay continues doing work she no longer needs.

In draft-21, cancellation abruptly closes the request stream's open directions. `STOP_SENDING` asks the peer to stop its sending direction; `RESET_STREAM` abandons the cancelling endpoint's own sending direction. A plain `FIN` only means that no more bytes will be sent in one direction. A subscriber can finish sending request messages while still expecting content, so `FIN` alone does not cancel the request. See [§6.4.2.2–3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-6.4.2.2).

When the publisher ends an established subscription, it closes the associated data streams, sends `PUBLISH_DONE`, and closes its request-stream direction. The data streams and request stream can arrive in different orders. Alice may therefore receive `PUBLISH_DONE` while some final object data is still on its way. See [§3.1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-3.1.1) and [§9.9](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-9.9).

Subscription lifetime also matters to authorization. If Alice's permission expires during the lecture, the service needs a policy for the subscription she already holds, as well as for any new request. Publication permission is separate: allowing Alice to watch must not allow her to replace the lecturer's content.
